notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes drawn from the sources retrieved, organised by tradition where distinct views emerged.

---

## Genesis 24:1-22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — *“By now Abraham was old and well along in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way.”*

- **Age.** Abraham was about 140 years old at this point (Isaac was born when Abraham was 100 [Gen 21:5], and Isaac was 40 at his marriage [Gen 25:20]). The repetition “old…advanced in age” underscores both his years and God’s faithful blessing (Gill, Pulpit, Ellicott).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **“Blessed in all things.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes the writer uses “Jehovah” (the LORD) here to show “how the God of redemption provided a bride for the heir of the promise.” Gill adds that this blessing was temporal — long life, riches, honour, children. Precept Austin expands: Abraham had material blessing (Gen 13:2), relational blessing (Isaac, the heir), spiritual blessing (tested faith, friendship with God), and covenant promises (Gen 12:2–3).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-24-commentary

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** even when God commanded Abraham to slay Isaac or took Sarah, “the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things”; blessing does not mean the absence of trials.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** “Moses, for the first time, adds his editorial comment that the patriarch has indeed been blessed… But this blessing cannot continue without offspring through Isaac.” The chapter moves from promise-fulfilled to promise-transmitted.
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/wife-isaac

- **Precept Austin (Evangelical):** Abraham’s advanced age adds urgency; securing a wife for Isaac ensures the covenant line leading to Messiah (cf. Gen 12:3; Mt 1:1–2; Gal 3:16).
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-24-commentary

---

### v. 2 — *“So Abraham instructed the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned, ‘Place your hand under my thigh…’”*

- **Identity of the servant.** Almost certainly Eliezer of Damascus, mentioned in Gen 15:2 as Abraham’s steward and former heir-presumptive. The term “eldest” (זָקֵן) is a title of honour — like sheikh, senatus, presbyter, sir (Pulpit). He had managed Abraham’s household for over 50 years (Gill).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **“Hand under my thigh.”** Multiple interpretations:
  - (1) The thigh as the source of posterity (cf. Gen 35:11; 46:26), pointing to Abraham’s descendants and ultimately Christ — the oath sworn by the coming seed (Keil, Kalisch, Lange — cited in Pulpit).
  - (2) A euphemism for the generative organ, bearing the sign of circumcision, making it an adjuration by the covenant sign (Jonathan, Jarchi, Tuch — cited in Pulpit).
  - (3) The thigh as symbolising lordship/authority; placing the hand under it an oath of fealty (Aben Ezra, Calvin, Murphy — cited in Pulpit).
  - (4) Adam Clarke (Methodist): the person binding himself touched the part bearing the sign of God’s covenant; a rite producing “reverence and godly fear” (cited in Enduring Word).
  - Gill notes this was also required later of Joseph by Jacob (Gen 47:29).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **JFB (older evangelical):** Abraham, being too old and as heir of the promise not at liberty to leave Canaan even temporarily, entrusted this delicate mission to Eliezer with a solemn oath.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 3 — *“…swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites…”*

- **The oath.** Abraham swears the servant by “the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth” — defining Jehovah as supreme Lord of the universe and sole Arbiter of human destiny (Pulpit). Gill notes Abraham always swore by this God (cf. Gen 14:22). The Targum of Jonathan renders it “the Word of the Lord God.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **“Not from the Canaanites.”** JFB says pastoral tribes required marriage within the tribe, but Abraham had “a far higher motive — a fear lest, if his son married into a Canaanitish family, he might be gradually led away from the true God.” The Pulpit Commentary adds Abraham was prompted by perception of Canaanite licentiousness, knowledge of their predicted doom, and “chiefly… a desire to preserve the purity of the promised seed.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** John Chrysostom comments that Abraham “acted in this from concern for the soul’s virtue and abhorrence of the wickedness of the [Canaanite] inhabitants.” This rule applies to the New Covenant — Christians are not to marry unbelievers (2 Cor 6:14a).
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/wife-isaac

- **Precept Austin (Evangelical):** the prohibition protects the Messianic line. Intermarriage with Canaanites was later codified in the Mosaic law (Ex 34:16; Deut 7:3).
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-24-commentary

---

### v. 4 — *“…but will go to my country and my kindred to take a wife for my son Isaac.”*

- **“My country and my kindred.”** Not Ur of the Chaldees specifically, but Mesopotamia broadly — the region beyond the Euphrates (Pulpit). Gill clarifies it was Haran in Mesopotamia, called “the city of Nahor” (v.10), where Nahor’s family still dwelt.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **Why relatives?** Gill notes that though Nahor’s family was not free from idolatry, they still knew the true God alongside their idols; a woman removed from that environment might be brought fully to pure religion. The family had sprung from Shem and was under God’s blessing.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **Gray’s Concise Commentary:** Abraham was under God’s guidance; “there was more than man’s wisdom or foresight in this transaction.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/genesis-24.html

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Abraham did not want a Canaanite wife for Isaac; the wife must come from among Abraham’s ancestors — a picture of the Father seeking a bride for His Son from His own people.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

### v. 5 — *“The servant asked him, ‘What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Shall I then take your son back to the land from which you came?’”*

- **The servant’s caution.** Pulpit Commentary says the servant spoke “not having the same faith as his master,” noting that prima facie it was reasonable to suppose the bride might refuse the long journey. Gill says the servant was being prudent — wanting to understand the scope of his oath before swearing.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **“Bring thy son again.”** Gill explains the expression “again” (though Isaac had never been there in person) by saying he was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham left, just as Levi paid tithes in Abraham (Heb 7:9–10).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

---

### v. 6 — *“Abraham replied, ‘Make sure that you do not take my son back there.’”*

- **“Beware thou.”** Abraham’s emphatic language — literally “beware for thyself” — underscores the gravity: under no pretext must Isaac leave Canaan (Pulpit).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Enduring Word:** Isaac, the son of promise, never once left the Promised Land. His bride must come to him. This principle was so important that if no woman would come, it was better for Isaac to remain unmarried.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

### v. 7 — *“‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who brought me from my father’s house… He will send His angel before you…’”*

- **Two grounds for confidence.** Pulpit: (1) Abraham had been called out of Mesopotamia and could not return without a like divine instruction; (2) God had sworn the land to his seed, which guaranteed Isaac’s place there and therefore the mission’s success.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **“His angel.”** Either a created angel employed in providence, or the uncreated Angel, the Son of God — Gill notes the servant himself later attributes his success wholly to “the LORD.”
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Abraham’s faith is explicit — he “never doubted that God would lead the servant to the right woman.” John Piper comments that Abraham was “tracing out for himself his own trajectories of obedience from what God had said and done in the past.”
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/wife-isaac
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-24-commentary

---

### v. 8 — *“‘And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine. Only do not take my son back there.’”*

- **Release clause.** Abraham’s instruction gave the servant liberty if, after doing all he could, the woman refused. Gill: Abraham was not doubting — he was persuaded God would make her willing — but made this provision to ease the servant’s mind.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **Pulpit:** “with almost feverish entreaty harping on the solemn refrain that on no account must Isaac leave the promised land, since in that would be the culmination of unbelief and disobedience.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 9 — *“So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore an oath to him concerning this matter.”*

- **The oath taken.** The servant, understanding his mission and satisfied on the points that touched his conscience, swore “to be true to his master and his mission, and to the hope and promise of the covenant” (Pulpit).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 10 — *“Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels and departed with all manner of good things from his master in hand. And he set out for Nahor’s hometown in Aram-naharaim.”*

- **Ten camels.** Rare in that era; owning ten reflected Abraham’s great wealth (cf. Job 1:3). The camels carried provisions, marriage presents, and spare animals (JFB, Constable).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

- **“All manner of good things.”** Literally “every good thing of his master in his hand” — meaning the servant selected the choicest valuables as presents for the bride and her family (Pulpit, Gill).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **Journey distance.** Straight-line about 500 miles (800 km); the common route about 900 miles (1,450 km) — roughly 17 days’ travel (Enduring Word citing Bunting’s Travels; Gill).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

---

### v. 11 — *“As evening approached, he made the camels kneel down near the well outside the town at the time when the women went out to draw water.”*

- **“Made the camels kneel.”** Camels are trained from youth to kneel for loading/unloading and rest. The Pulpit Commentary notes “the action is literally kneeling… and this the camel is taught to do from his youth.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **The well at evening.** In the East, wells were typically outside the city; women drew water both morning and evening. The servant stationed himself strategically — a stranger seeking information would go to the well when women gathered (JFB, Pulpit, Gill).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 12 — *“‘O LORD, God of my master Abraham,’ he prayed, ‘please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.’”*

- **First recorded prayer for specific guidance.** Constable notes this is the first instance in Scripture of someone praying for providential guidance in a specific matter. The servant addresses God as “God of my master Abraham” — not his own God, but Abraham’s — because he comes on his master’s business (Gill, Constable).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

- **“Show kindness (hesed) to my master.”** The servant’s personal humility and fidelity are striking — he seeks nothing for himself. The Pulpit Commentary calls this “a beautiful example of piety and of the fruits of Abraham’s care for the souls of his household (Gen 18:19).”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** The servant’s faith is practical — he prays for success yet sets a clear, objective standard beforehand, a crucial safeguard against manipulating circumstances to determine God’s will.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

### v. 13 — *“‘Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water.’”*

- **Presenting himself.** The phrase “Behold me standing” (v.43) reflects the servant’s posture of expectant faith — he has positioned himself, acted practically, and now waits on God (Pulpit).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 14 — *“‘Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, “Please let down your jar that I may drink,” and who responds, “Drink, and I will water your camels as well” — let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.’”*

- **The sign.** The Pulpit Commentary says the sign was the “kindly disposition of the maiden” — not only prompt compliance but generous exceeding of the request. It is probable the servant was “led to choose this sign… by that Divine inspiration and guidance of which he had been assured (v.7).”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Remarkable but possible.** Enduring Word: the servant asked for a sign that was remarkable but humanly possible; he didn’t tempt God by demanding a miracle. Yet the task was daunting: a camel can drink up to 20 gallons (80 litres); ten camels meant at least an hour of hard manual labour.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

- **Character, not appearance.** The servant “cared nothing about the woman’s appearance. He wanted a woman of character, a woman whom God had chosen.” The sign tested kindness, hospitality, industry, and willingness to help a stranger (Constable).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

- **Caution about signs.** Gray’s Concise Commentary warns it is “ill-advised to leave the decisions of life to the arbitrament of signs, and grievous errors have arisen from accrediting God with the outcome of them.” When we have God’s Word, Spirit, providence, and prayer, “it is expected and doubtless salutary that we bear the responsibility of our own decisions.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/genesis-24.html

- **Gill:** the servant sought a woman who was careful, industrious, humane, courteous to strangers, humble, and condescending — not proud or arrogant.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

---

### v. 15 — *“Before the servant had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor.”*

- **Answered before finished.** This is linked to Isaiah 65:24: “Before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear” (Enduring Word, Pulpit). The Pulpit notes from v.45 that the prayer was offered “in his heart,” not aloud.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** John Calvin says this fact “shows that God moves to aid us prior to our supplications… God proves for all His people by unquestionable examples, that although the event may not immediately respond to our wishes, the prayers of his people are never in vain.”
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/enter-rebekah

- **Rebekah’s lineage.** She was the granddaughter of Nahor, Abraham’s brother — exactly meeting the kinship requirement (JFB). Her name in Hebrew sounds like the word for “blessing,” making her fitting to join the covenant family (Ligonier).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/enter-rebekah

---

### v. 16 — *“Now the girl was very beautiful, a virgin who had not had relations with any man. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again.”*

- **“Very beautiful.”** The Bible is given to understatement; when it says “very beautiful to behold,” Rebekah was indeed exceptionally attractive (Enduring Word). She joins Sarah, Rachel, Abigail, Bathsheba, Esther and others specifically noted as beautiful. The Pulpit notes the Hebrew is “good of countenance,” like Sarah (Gen 12:11) and Rachel (Gen 29:17).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **“A virgin.”** The Hebrew *bethulah* means one separated and secluded; the repetition “neither had any man known her” is emphatic, underscoring her purity (Pulpit).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Went down… came up.** Wells in the East were often in wadis with steps down to the water — an arduous task, making her subsequent offer to water ten camels even more remarkable (Pulpit, JFB).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

### v. 17 — *“So the servant ran to meet her and said, ‘Please let me have a little water from your jar.’”*

- **“Ran to meet her.”** Enduring Word: the servant did not think it unspiritual to introduce himself; he acted. “Prayer is no substitute for action.” Yet he asked only for water for himself — he did nothing to prompt her to offer water for the camels.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

- **A “little” water.** Gill notes the servant’s modesty — he asks for only “a little water,” making the test all the more stringent since Rebekah’s generosity would have to go far beyond what was requested.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

---

### v. 18 — *“‘Drink, my lord,’ she replied, and she quickly lowered her jar to her hands and gave him a drink.”*

- **“My lord.”** Rebekah’s address with utmost politeness and cheerful animation. The Pulpit notes “Rebekah’s address to the servant will be given you in the exact idiom by the first gentle Rebekah you ask water from” in the East.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **“Quickly lowered.”** Her haste in serving shows eager hospitality, akin to Abraham’s reception of the angels in Gen 18:1–8 (Ligonier).
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-sovereign-favor

---

### v. 19 — *“After she had given him a drink, she said, ‘I will also draw water for your camels, until they have had enough to drink.’”*

- **The sign fulfilled.** Rebekah volunteers — unprompted — the very words the servant had specified. The Pulpit Commentary says this shows “the kindly disposition within her bosom was not simply the reflex of national customs, but the invisible sun beaming through her mind, and freely bringing forward the blossoms of sterling goodness” (Kalisch).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Gill:** her offer demonstrates she was not proud or disdainful, but humble, courteous, generous, and willing to labour.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/24.htm

---

### v. 20 — *“And she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran back to the well to draw water, until she had drawn water for all his camels.”*

- **“Quickly… ran.”** Her haste is emphasised twice. The Pulpit Commentary describes the trough as a stone gutter beside the well. She had to go repeatedly from well to trough — exhausting work.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **The sheer volume.** Camels, though famous for enduring thirst, drink enormous quantities when water is available (Kalisch, cited in Pulpit). Constable estimates each camel could drink up to 25 gallons.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-24.html

- **Enduring Word:** “She quickly emptied her pitcher into the trough, ran back to the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.” She did the hard work — not just talked about it.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

---

### v. 21 — *“Meanwhile, the man watched her silently to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success.”*

- **“Wondering at her… held his peace.”** The Hebrew conveys gazing with attention, amazed and astonished (Pulpit). He remained silent — the customary posture for expecting or receiving divine direction (cf. Lev 10:3; Ps 39:2; Acts 11:18).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Waiting for full confirmation.** Enduring Word: the servant “did not stop her” from the hard work; he wanted to see if she had a servant’s heart, not merely a servant’s talk. “For some, it is much easier to talk like a servant than to actually serve.”
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** “His silence does betray some amazement that God has moved so quickly, a feeling we may likewise experience when the Lord meets our needs so abundantly.”
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/enter-rebekah

---

### v. 22 — *“And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels.”*

- **The gifts.** The “ring” (נֶזֶם, *nezem*) is specifically a **nose-ring**, not an earring — the side cartilage (or sometimes central wall) of the nose was pierced for it (cf. Ezekiel 16:11–12). Delitzsch notes “the nose-ring is now the usual engagement present among the Bedouins” (Pulpit, JFB).
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/genesis-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-22.htm

- **Weight.** A *beka* was half a shekel (cf. Exodus 38:26) — about 5.7 grams of gold for the nose-ring. The two bracelets (צָמִיד, *tsamid*, from “to bind/fasten”) together weighed ten shekels — about 114 grams of gold. These were substantial gifts, signalling the wealth of the master (Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-22.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

- **Not a bridal gift yet.** Keil & Delitzsch note these were placed on her “not as a bridal gift, but in return for her kindness.” The formal bridal gifts come later after the family’s consent (v.53).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/24-22.htm

- **Enduring Word (typology):** This prefigures the Church receiving rich gifts from the Father through the Holy Spirit even before the marriage to the Son — the bride is chosen, called, and lavished with gifts.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-24/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The production of the presents and the servant’s questions indicate “he already entertained the belief that he looked upon the object of his search.”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-24.html

---

## Distinctive Tradition Emphases (Summary)

| Tradition | Emphasis in Genesis 24:1–22 |
|-----------|----------------------------|
| **Reformed/Presbyterian** (Ligonier, Calvin) | God’s meticulous providence; prayer answered before finished; covenant preservation; typology of Christ and the Church via a faithful servant; the bride must be from the covenant community. |
| **Baptist** (Spurgeon) | Blessing coexists with trials; the servant’s self-effacing devotion (“my master” 22 times) models Christian service; the urgency of the messenger refusing delay. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik) | Practical faith and Spirit-led guidance; the servant’s prayer as a model for discerning God’s will; typology of Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and Church; the difference between “servant’s talk” and a “servant’s heart.” |
| **Evangelical** (Precept Austin, Constable) | Providence in ordinary events; biblical stewardship modelled by Eliezer; Abraham’s faith expressed in practical obedience; the longest chapter in Genesis signals the importance of securing the covenant line. |
| **Older commentaries** (Gill, Pulpit, JFB, Ellicott, Henry) | Historical and linguistic detail; multiple interpretations of “hand under thigh”; emphasis on the oath’s covenant significance; the servant as a model of piety. |

*(No distinct Catholic, Orthodox, or modern-scholarship views on this specific passage were retrievable from the permitted sites within the search limits.)*
